summary: Learners aged 7-12 build and interpret force diagrams: forces shown as labelled arrows on one chosen object, where arrow LENGTH shows relative size and DIRECTION shows which way the force acts. They use diagrams to decide whether forces are balanced (equal, opposite arrows, no resultant) or unbalanced (unequal arrows, a resultant), draw a single resultant arrow, and link the diagram to a prediction of motion. The core habit to instil is the free-body / replacement principle: pick ONE object and draw only the forces acting ON it, with arrow tails attached to the body (not floating in mid-air) and each arrow labelled by force type. Key conceptual targets include that balanced forces do not mean 'no forces' and do not necessarily mean 'stationary' (constant-velocity coasting also has balanced forces), that a resultant force determines how an object's motion CHANGES (its acceleration) relative to how it is already moving, and that motion does not require a forward force.
misconceptions: Drawing arrows 'hanging in mid-air', detached from the object, or unclear which object a force acts on (so it's impossible to tell push-of-A-on-B from B-on-A).
Motion implies a force: drawing a forward force arrow on anything that is moving, even at constant velocity (impetus).
Confusing the direction of velocity with the direction of the net force (Viennot's juggler task — persists after instruction).
Believing balanced forces must mean the object is stationary (not realising constant-velocity motion also has balanced forces).
Ignoring arrow length (all arrows drawn the same), or over-demanding an exact scale that obscures the physics for young learners.
Reading the diagram as a literal picture of the scene rather than as a representation of vector forces.

activities.title: Arrow editor: forces that drive the crate
steps: Start from a crate with NO arrows drawn on it.

Add force arrows to the crate; set each arrow's length and direction (for example by dragging a handle at the arrow's tip), with every arrow's tail locked to the crate — only forces acting ON the crate are allowed.
Make two opposing arrows equal in length and predict, then check, what the crate does; then make one arrow longer and predict/check again, stating the crate's current motion each time.
Read or draw the resultant as a single arrow summarising the net force.

Attempt the 'coasting' challenge: a crate is already sliding to the right on a surface with negligible horizontal friction — decide what arrows (if any) it needs to keep gliding at steady speed, then test it.
Label each arrow by force type (e.g. push, friction, weight, support).
activities.insight: The arrows cause the CHANGE in motion (the acceleration): equal opposing arrows give no change (an object stays still if it was still, or keeps gliding at constant speed if it was already moving), while unequal arrows give a resultant whose direction determines how the motion changes — a box already moving the resultant's way speeds up, a box moving the opposite way first slows. A still-moving crate kept at steady speed with no net forward force overturns 'motion needs a forward force'.

activities.title: Cardboard arrows: build the diagram by hand first
steps: Use physical 'cardboard arrows' (cut to different lengths) laid onto a picture or model of one object to build up its force diagram before drawing on paper.
Place each arrow so its tail sits on the object and point it the way the force acts; pick a longer piece for a bigger force.
For a pair of interacting objects, build the diagram for ONE object at a time, replacing the other object with the force arrow it exerts.
Describe out loud which object each arrow acts on and name the force type.
activities.insight: A force diagram is a representation of one chosen object with the forces acting ON it; building it physically makes the replacement principle and arrow attachment concrete before committing to pencil.

activities.title: Interpret and construct: the resting book and the pushed box
steps: Look at a force diagram of a box being pushed to the right across the floor (already moving right): a long arrow right labelled 'push' and a shorter arrow left labelled 'friction'. State what the lengths and directions tell you about what the box is doing.
Identify the resultant's direction and justify it from the arrow lengths.
Draw the force arrows for a book resting still on a table, attaching each arrow to the book and labelling it.
Redraw the box with push and friction EQUAL and say what the box is now doing.
Answer: if the friction arrow became longer than the push, what would happen to the box that is moving right?
activities.insight: Reading a diagram: the longer opposing arrow sets the resultant's direction → unbalanced → the motion changes that way relative to how the box is already moving. Constructing a diagram: even a still object has forces — weight down AND the table's support (normal) force up, equal and opposite (balanced), both starting on the book — so 'still' is drawn with balanced arrows, not a blank.

activities.title: Spot the error / match the motion (quick checks)
steps: Error-finding: given a diagram, spot the arrow that does not start on the object ('spot the mid-air arrow') and redraw it correctly.
Choose from outcomes for 'balanced or unbalanced — what happens next?', including a 'must be stationary' option to be rejected when the object is already moving.
Match each diagram to its motion description.
Identify the resultant for a given pair or set of arrows.
Sketch the arrows onto a pictured object for a described situation, stating the object's current motion.
activities.insight: Fluent learners consistently attach arrows to the object, read length as magnitude and direction as the way the force acts, and know balanced forces can accompany steady motion, not only rest.

checkQuestion: Look at this force diagram of a box being pushed across the floor: a long arrow points right labelled 'push', and a shorter arrow points left labelled 'friction'. What do the lengths and directions of the two arrows tell you about what the box is doing? Then draw the force arrows for a book resting still on a table.
checkAnswer: The two arrows are opposite (push right, friction left) and the push arrow is LONGER, so the forces are unbalanced with a resultant to the right — the box speeds up / moves right. For the resting book: two arrows ON the book — weight pointing DOWN and the table's support (normal) force pointing UP — equal in length (balanced), both starting on the book, so it stays still.
